We are Voyager Celebi, a team of students from Türkiye, at İzmir Kâtip Çelebi University. Inspired by NASA's Voyager missions and Kâtip Çelebi's legacy in cartography, we aim to develop an interactive Mars map using NASA data for safe navigation and scientific exploration.

From Earth's Maps to Martian Paths...
summary:
What if the shortest route on Mars is not the best route?

MarsEye is an interactive 3D exploration and mission-planning platform designed to make Martian navigation more informed, transparent, and science-driven.

Developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, MarsEye combines real Mars-derived topographic data, NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX imagery, and Mars Odyssey THEMIS thermal observations within a pilot region of Gale Crater.

Our terrain-aware A* algorithm evaluates slope, surface roughness, elevation gain, and experimental thermal costs to generate alternative routes for rovers and astronauts. Users can select starting points, destinations, and scientific investigation sites, compare routes under different mobility constraints, and optimize multi-stop missions.

Unlike a conventional map, MarsEye transforms scientific observations into interactive mission-planning decisions, allowing users to understand not only where a route goes, but why it was selected.

By integrating open planetary data, explainable navigation, and scientific waypoint planning, MarsEye offers a foundation for future autonomous exploration research, mission simulations, and planetary science education.
details:
MarsEye — Intelligent Mars Exploration and Mission Planning

The Problem

On Mars, the shortest route is not necessarily the most suitable one. Steep slopes, rough terrain, elevation changes, thermal conditions, and scientific objectives can significantly influence navigation decisions.

MarsEye addresses the challenge of transforming complex planetary observations into accessible and explainable route-planning decisions for future exploration scenarios.

Our Solution

MarsEye is an interactive 3D Mars exploration and mission-planning prototype developed for a 1 × 1 km pilot region in Gale Crater, near Mount Sharp.

Our platform combines three real Mars-derived datasets:

  • Topographic data: A digital elevation model processed into a 200 × 200 navigation grid at approximately 5 m resolution.
  • Optical data: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX imagery for visual terrain exploration.
  • Thermal data: Mars Odyssey THEMIS infrared observations, including nighttime brightness temperatures measured in Kelvin at approximately 100 m native resolution.

The platform integrates these datasets into an interactive 3D environment where users can explore terrain, inspect scientific parameters, and plan missions.

Intelligent Navigation Algorithms

At the core of MarsEye is an enhanced A* path-planning algorithm.

Unlike a distance-only approach, our experimental risk-aware model evaluates terrain slope, surface roughness, elevation gain, and an optional thermal penalty.

Different mobility profiles allow the system to calculate routes for rovers and astronauts using different traversability constraints and cost weights.

The current prototype compares three alternatives: a distance-oriented shortest feasible route, an astronaut risk-aware route, and a rover risk-aware route.

The interface displays route distances, slopes, elevation changes, roughness, and available thermal statistics, making the trade-offs between routes understandable.

Scientific Mission Planning

MarsEye also supports multi-stop scientific missions.

Users can select a starting point, a destination, and up to five proposed scientific investigation locations directly on the 3D terrain.

The system calculates routes between these locations and can optimize their visiting order based on actual terrain-dependent route costs.

This transforms conventional point-to-point navigation into a more flexible scientific mission-planning workflow.

Innovation and Impact

MarsEye's innovation is not the invention of a new shortest-path algorithm, but the integration of multiple planetary datasets, terrain-aware navigation, different mobility profiles, scientific waypoint optimization, and explainable route analytics into one interactive environment.

Our intended users include planetary science students, robotics researchers, mission-planning teams, and educators.

MarsEye demonstrates how publicly available NASA data can support transparent engineering decisions and exploratory mission simulations.

Technologies Used

We developed MarsEye using Python, NumPy, FastAPI, JavaScript, Three.js, HTML, CSS, Git, and GitHub, supported by scientific raster-processing tools.

Python handles scientific data processing, route calculations, and mission optimization. Three.js provides interactive 3D terrain visualization, while JavaScript connects user interactions to the navigation system.

Validation and Future Development

The prototype has been tested using real Mars-derived terrain data, with automated tests for navigation and mission-planning functionality.

The current models remain experimental. Terrain and thermal cost weights are not NASA-certified safety criteria, and some data provenance and geospatial validation work remains.

Future development will focus on higher-resolution hazard mapping, energy-aware navigation, uncertainty modeling, robotic simulation, and validation using physical mobile robots.

Our long-term vision is to turn MarsEye into an extensible research platform where planetary data becomes actionable, scientifically informed mission-planning insight.
